rationale: The BOOK ENTRY defines 'seed' as a generative word or life planted to reproduce after its kind, then distributes the referent by context: word in the sower, children in the tares, Messiah as the promised Seed, and one planted person growing into a house/people/nation-tree. Every one of these printed assertions is carried directly by the cited texts: Gen 1:11-12 supplies the 'after his kind' reproductive mechanic verbatim; Matt 13:19 ties the sower's seed to 'the word of the kingdom... sown in his heart' (confirmed by Luke 8:11 in the chapter); Matt 13:38 states explicitly 'the good seed are the children of the kingdom'; Gen 3:15 with Gal 3:16 identifies the promised Seed as Christ; and Isa 51:2 ('I called him alone... and increased him') with Matt 13:31-32 (least seed becoming a tree in which birds lodge) grounds the one-person-to-nation-tree movement, further corroborated by Ezekiel 17 and Daniel 4 in the supporting chapters. The strongest counters (seed = Word of God exclusively, or seed = Messianic offspring exclusively) are each narrower slices of the entry's umbrella and each fails texts the entry explains: a word-only reading cannot absorb Matt 13:38's explicit 'the good seed are the children,' and a Messiah-only reading cannot absorb Matt 13:19/Luke 8:11. The entry's unifying genus ('generative word or life reproducing after its kind') is exactly what Gen 1:11-12 licenses and is the only formulation among the alternatives that explains all cited texts without remainder.
book_core_identification: Seed is a generative word or life planted to reproduce after its kind, whose specific referent is context-assigned: God's word (sower), children of a spiritual family (wheat and tares), the Messiah (the promised Seed), and a planted person who grows into a house, people, or nation.
book_secondary_elaborations: In the parable of the sower the seed is God's word (Matt 13:19; Luke 8:11).
In the wheat and tares the seed is children — of the kingdom or of the wicked one (Matt 13:38; Gen 3:15).
The promised Seed is the Messiah (Gen 3:15; Gal 3:16).
One planted person may grow into a house, people, or nation-tree (Isa 51:2; Matt 13:31-32; John 12:24).
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's reading of the leaven parable as corrupt doctrine infiltrating (against the traditional gospel-permeation reading) is a chapter claim, not printed in the entry.
The chapter's inverted reading of the treasure-in-the-field (God as buyer, people as treasure) is chapter-only.
The Daniel 12:4 application ('running to and fro' = searching Scripture with modern tools) is chapter-only and speculative.
The claim that the disciples were culpably accountable because the symbol system was uniformly established across the OT is a chapter-level methodological thesis, not a printed entry assertion.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Seed symbolizes primarily the Word of God/gospel sown in hearts (per Luke 8:11, Jesus' own key), with offspring/Messiah and other senses treated as separate, unrelated usages rather than instances of one generative principle — i.e., there is no unified 'seed' symbol, only discrete context-bound meanings, of which 'word of God' is the definitional one (Responses A and C).
counter_core_identification: Seed = the word of God/gospel planted in human hearts; other uses (offspring, Messiah, kingdom growth) are distinct meanings, not parts of one definition.
material_core_denial: The counter would deny that a single generative definition legitimately spans word, children, Messiah, and nation-growth, insisting the primary and defining sense is the word of God alone; but it does not deny any specific identification the entry makes in its own context (it affirms seed=word in the sower, and concedes seed=offspring/Messiah as a recognized alternative), so both cores can be true of the same referents.
counter_case: Luke 8:11 is Scripture's only explicit 'the seed is X' definition, giving 'word of God' unique definitional authority.
Treating seed as one unified symbol risks flattening genuinely distinct usages (agricultural, genealogical, parabolic).
Response C notes there is no settled single symbolic meaning, which cuts against any one-sentence glossary definition.
book_explanatory_advantages: Gen 1:11-12 supplies a genus ('seed... after his kind') that explains why both a word and a lineage can be 'seed': each reproduces its source's nature — the entry alone explains the shared mechanic behind the divergent referents.
Matt 13:38 ('the good seed are the children of the kingdom') is Jesus' own second key, which a word-only definition cannot accommodate but the entry prints explicitly.
Isa 51:2 plus Matt 13:31-32 (and Ezek 17/Dan 4 in evidence) explain the person-to-nation-tree growth pattern the entry asserts, which no common response integrates.
John 12:24 (seed as a life that dies and multiplies) fits 'generative life planted' and bridges word-seed and person-seed, which the entry's genus predicts.
The entry reconciles the two competing 'primary' meanings of Responses A/C versus B/D rather than arbitrating between them.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Luke 8:11's explicit definition gives the word-of-God sense the strongest single proof-text.
The counter matches the most common devotional and homiletical usage.
decisive_sources: Genesis 1:11-12 (KJV excerpt) — establishes the 'after his kind' reproductive genus printed in the entry.
Matthew 13:38 (KJV excerpt) — Jesus explicitly identifies good seed as children, defeating any word-only counter-definition.
Matthew 13:19 with Luke 8:11 (chapter) — establishes seed = word in the sower.
Galatians 3:16 with Genesis 3:15 — establishes the promised Seed as Christ.
Isaiah 51:2 with Matthew 13:31-32 and Ezekiel 17:22-24/Daniel 4:12,22 (chapter evidence) — establishes one planted person growing into a nation-tree.
unresolved_objections: Whether a glossary should present one unified genus rather than enumerate discrete senses is a taxonomic preference; the entry's genus is supported but not the only defensible organization.
The 'nation-tree' terminus leans partly on chapter-level tree symbolism (Ezek 17, Dan 4) not printed with the entry, though Isa 51:2 and Matt 13:31-32 are printed and carry the claim adequately.
